subtype: Approach: open-ended distance with no end date [Pitfall]
passage: Nkechi's last term in Lagos ended in four months. Kwame's programme in Toronto had a year left. They talked every night, cheerful and sweet, about films, families, and food. Neither said the word "after". Once Kwame started: "When you finish, do you..." and Nkechi said quickly, "Let's not spoil tonight." The silence that followed was a small stone. The next month it got bigger. Nkechi began to answer late. Kwame started to sound careful. Each privately guessed what the other would say, and each guess was worse than the truth might have been. By the third month, their conversations were shorter and politer. In the fourth month, an argument about a delayed message ended with "You never plan anything", and the real subject was still unspoken.

qa.q: How many months did Nkechi have left in Lagos?
What was Nkechi feeling when Kwame began the sentence 'When you finish, do you...'?
qa.a: Nkechi felt afraid of the answer and wanted to protect the evening, so the subject was cut off quickly.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the couple use, and why?
qa.a: They could set a calm time to talk about where each would live after graduation, because leaving it unspoken let hope turn into guesses.

qa.q: How might Kwame see Nkechi's late answers?
qa.a: Kwame sounds careful and guesses at the reason, so Kwame may read the delay as distance without knowing the real fear behind it.

grounding: Shows a couple with no end date who never discuss where they will live afterwards, so unspoken fear turns hope into resentment.
